strengths: The task is relevant and useful: editing an image using only a target emotion could simplify creative workflows. The manuscript clearly motivates why changing emotional content can require more than color or style transfer.

EmoPair provides a potentially useful resource comprising 331,595 relabeled editing pairs and 6,949 newly generated pairs. The manuscript credits the underlying datasets and models and describes its curation pipeline.

The human study provides evidence beyond classifier scores: EmoEditor receives approximately 56% average preference against the five baselines. Qualitative examples demonstrate meaningful changes to objects, expressions, and atmosphere.
The manuscript explicitly acknowledges evaluator bias, semantic preservation failures, and potential emotional manipulation risks. These disclosures strengthen the presentation.
weaknesses: The principal quantitative evidence is strongly coupled to the optimization procedure. The same predictor P labels or filters training data, selects outputs over up to 30 editing iterations, and supplies EMR, ESR, and ENRD. Table 1 shows EMR falling from 50.20% to 5.06% without the critic. This demonstrates dependence on classifier-guided inference, but does not establish comparable improvement in human emotional responses. Independent evaluation and human ablations are needed.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed editor's contribution from its additional training and inference budget. InstructPix2Pix receives a single emotion word, while EmoEditor receives specialized training and repeated classifier-guided editing. Applying the same selection procedure and comparable generation budgets to the baselines would be informative. The directly relevant Affective Image Filter is discussed but not experimentally compared.

The architectural and reasoning claims exceed the demonstrated novelty. The implementation starts from InstructPix2Pix and introduces an emotion MLP and alignment loss. Because the emotion embedding depends only on the target category, it is identical across source images with that target; its alignment does not itself demonstrate source-specific instruction reasoning. Comparisons against simple learned class embeddings and an equivalently fine-tuned InstructPix2Pix would clarify the contribution.

Two central mathematical descriptions require clarification. Section 3.2 defines the noised latent from the source image, without showing how the paired target image enters the denoising objective; as written, this describes source reconstruction rather than supervised target editing. Section 4 defines ESR using KL divergence from a predicted distribution to an exact one-hot vector, which is generally infinite. These could be notation errors, but the implemented training objective and finite metric definition must be specified before the results can be assessed reliably.

Dataset quality and semantic preservation are insufficiently validated. Most pairs receive automatic emotion labels from a predictor reporting 73% accuracy on EmoSet, with no independent annotation audit on the constructed dataset. Some generated training examples substantially replace source content—for example, the caged dog becomes a building in Figure S3. Human evaluation measures emotional preference rather than preservation, leaving a central task requirement weakly supported.

The human evidence supports a modest, qualified advantage. Preference over LMS is 54% online and 49% in the small laboratory study; negative-to-positive preference against LMS is approximately chance online. Only 27% of online participants pass the controls, warranting clearer analysis of participant exclusion and uncertainty accounting for repeated ratings. Quantitative evaluation also concentrates on cross-valence transitions; within-valence discrimination and neutral-image generalization receive only qualitative support.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the promised release. Section S2.2 omits learning rate, batch size, training duration, and important sampling settings. Runtime and the distribution of required editing iterations are also absent, making the practical cost of the critic and comparisons with LMS difficult to assess.
